You plan replenishment orders for one distribution centre. Read the objective, the master data
(the network as of the first week), the messages received so far (they report changes since
then) and the inventory position, then decide how many units to order from each plant this
week. Order a SKU only from a plant that makes it.
Answer with JSON only:
{"orders": [{"plant": "<plant id>", "sku": "<sku id>", "quantity": <number>}]}

Objective: keep the total cost over the remaining weeks as low as possible. The simulation ends after week 52; units that arrive later are paid for but never used. Actual weekly demand varies randomly around the forecast, typically within about 20%. Total cost is the purchase price of every unit accepted, plus holding cost on every unit in stock at the end of each week (0.5 per unit per week), plus backlog cost on every unit of demand not yet served at the end of each week (25 per unit per week). Unserved demand stays as backlog until it is served. An order arrives after its lane's lead time, rounded up to whole weeks. A plant ships at most its weekly capacity, shared across the SKUs it makes; a suspended supplier ships nothing, and a restricted supplier ships 50% of its plants' capacity. A plant refuses what it cannot ship. Lots on quality hold cannot be used. Orders can only be placed for a SKU at a plant that makes it.

Objective: keep the total cost over the remaining weeks as low as possible. The simulation ends after week 52; units that arrive later are paid for but never used. Actual weekly demand varies randomly around the forecast, typically within about 20%. A plant ships at most its weekly capacity, shared across the SKUs it makes; a suspended supplier ships nothing, and a restricted supplier ships 50% of its plants' capacity. A plant ships at most its weekly capacity, shared across the SKUs it makes; a suspended supplier ships nothing, and a restricted supplier ships 50% of its plants' capacity.
